sentences.text: Two more details of Rule seventeen, and then a thought of my own.
First, when a power-driven stand-on vessel acts on her own in a crossing situation, she should not, if the circumstances allow, turn to port for a vessel on her own port side.
The other boat is on your port side, and she’s late, but she finally turns to starboard to go behind you.
If you turn to port at the same moment, you turn straight into her.
So turn to starboard, or slow down, or stop.
Second, nothing the stand-on vessel does relieves the give-way vessel of her obligation.
She’s still responsible for keeping out of the way.
Keeping your course and speed means being predictable.
Rule two is still there, and no captain was ever praised for standing on into a collision.
Crossing: the boat with the other on her starboard side gives way.
And for the stand-on vessel: shall hold, may act, shall act.
Next time, we’ll climb the pecking order and see who gives way to whom when the vessels aren’t alike.
